pages.text: The rain came down like a drum roll, and the roads of the city turned to rivers. The trotro was packed with passengers on their way to the inter-school quiz. Patrick Attipoe, from Palm Crest Estate, sat stiffly near the door. His driver had fallen sick, and his father’s car was in the garage. “Is this normal?” he whispered, holding his bag on his knees. Halima, beside him, smiled. “Welcome to the city,” she said.

pages.alt: A packed trotro in heavy rain with passengers holding bags and a boy sitting stiffly near the door.

pages.text: The mate, the conductor who collected fares, leaned in. “Fare, fare!” he called. Patrick held out a big note. “I do not have change,” said the mate, “but your friends can help.” Theophilus, across the aisle, passed some coins. “Pay it forward,” he said. Patrick blushed and thanked him. “Please move in, please!” called the mate. A woman shifted to make room. Nobody complained, and Patrick learned something about patience.

pages.text: Samuel, a boy of twelve, squeezed in with his bag of sachet water. “Cold water, cold water!” he called, passing it hand to hand with a smile. He sold in the mornings and went to school in the afternoons, and today the rain had stopped him from going. Patrick had never spoken to a hawker. “How much?” he asked. “One cedi,” said Samuel. “For you, one cedi and a smile.” Patrick laughed and bought two.

pages.text: After an hour, the trotro was still stuck. Patrick reached into his pocket, and his face fell. “My phone,” he said. “It is gone.” The woman next to him frowned. “That boy who passed around the water,” she said loudly, pointing at Samuel. “He was close to you.” The whole bus fell silent. Samuel’s face turned grey. “I did not take it,” he said quietly. “I swear.”

pages.text: Halima stood up. “Please, let us not accuse anyone without evidence,” she said calmly. “Patrick, when did you last use it?” “Just before the second bridge,” he said. Theophilus nodded. “Then let us look under the seats first.” Passengers moved their bags and feet. Samuel searched with the rest, his hands trembling. “We must be fair,” said Halima. “Looking comes before blaming.”

pages.text: Theophilus found it, face down in the gap between two seats, the screen glowing. “Here!” he cried. “It slipped out of your pocket when you moved over.” A sigh of relief passed through the bus. The woman’s face fell. “I am sorry, young man,” she said to Samuel. “I should not have said it.” Samuel nodded. “It is all right, Madam,” he said, “but it did hurt.” The woman pressed a few coins into his hand. “For your water,” she said.

pages.text: As the trotro finally rolled forward, Patrick turned to Samuel. “I am sorry too,” he said. “I did not say anything when she pointed at you. I should have.” Samuel shrugged. “You were scared,” he said. “But next time, speak.” Patrick nodded. “Next time,” he said. By the time they reached the quiz hall, the four had swapped names, numbers and plans to study together. They had crossed four worlds in a single bus.

pages.text: In English class the next day, Halima showed how to report what was said. “Direct speech uses quotation marks,” she said. “‘Please move in,’ said the mate. Reported speech changes the words: ‘The mate asked the passengers to move in.’ We drop the quotation marks, change the pronouns and usually move the verb back in time. So ‘I did not take it,’ said Samuel becomes ‘Samuel said that he had not taken it.’” Patrick wrote it in his notebook.

Reported speech changes the words: ‘The mate asked the passengers to move in.’ We drop the quotation marks, change the pronouns and usually move the verb back in time.
So ‘I did not take it,’ said Samuel becomes ‘Samuel said that he had not taken it.’” Patrick wrote it in his notebook.

pages.text: Exam-safe tip: in reported speech, check three things: the quotation marks, the pronouns and the tense. “‘I am sorry,’ said Patrick” becomes “Patrick said that he was sorry.” Always begin with a capital letter, and always use full words in the answer. And remember Samuel: the evidence comes before the accusation. The end.
